about: Step 2b (research): one verdict per candidate, written by the checker after reading the evidence fetched in 02a and, where that was not enough, a web search or the primary text. Fields: status (verified | corrected | unverified | dropped); checked (what was read); note (what it says); fix (fields replaced in the event). Checked by a Claude Code agent with web search on 2026-11-03; a scholar should spot-check, starting with the corrected and unverified rows. 'added' at the end lists events the checker added because the draft left gaps.

plato-phaedrus.note: Composition c. 370 BCE confirmed. The draft said the dialogue 'closes with' the myth of Theuth and Thamus; the myth comes near the end (274c), and the dialogue closes with a prayer to Pan.

fix.description: In this dialogue Socrates and the young Phaedrus walk outside the walls of Athens and discuss love, rhetoric, and the soul. Near its end Socrates tells the myth of Theuth and Thamus, a critique of writing as a text that cannot answer back when it is questioned.

confucius-analects.checked: Wikipedia lead; Legge's 1861 translation on Project Gutenberg (#4094) for the quote
confucius-analects.note: Scholarly consensus: compiled over the Warring States period (475–221 BCE), reaching final form in the mid-Han dynasty. The draft's 5th–3rd century range was close; the Han final form was missing. The Legge quotation of 1.1 matches the Gutenberg text exactly.

fix.date_display: Warring States period (475–221 BCE), final form in the Han dynasty
fix.quote_attribution: Analects 1.1, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861)

shelley-frankenstein-1818.note: Publication on 1 January 1818, anonymously, confirmed. The quotation was given in its 1831 wording; the 1818 text, which the citation names, has a comma after 'November'.

fix.quote: It was on a dreary night of November, that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.

added.title: "On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots"
added.who: Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, and Margaret Mitchell (as 'Shmargaret Shmitchell')
added.description: The paper argues that ever-larger language models carry environmental, financial, and social costs, and that fluent output can be mistaken for meaning. Its phrase 'stochastic parrot' became shorthand in arguments about whether language models understand anything.
added.checked: Wikipedia, 'Stochastic parrot'; web search (Quote Investigator citation, ACM DOI)
added.note: Added by the checker: the draft had Bender and Koller's octopus paper but not this one.
